extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, academic-publishing stakeholders, and readers interested in retractions and publication ethics
extracted.subtask_description: A report on Springer Nature's disclosure of retraction counts and a summary of the types of integrity problems, triggers for investigations, and publisher responsibilities for quality control and correcting the record. Useful for people assessing what signals or processes prompt investigations and retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-acceptance rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher applies rigour prior to acceptance to help maintain the accuracy and integrity of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer Nature states they apply rigour prior to acceptance as part of maintaining research integrity; this implies robust checks during editorial handling and peer review but the article does not list the specific checks. Use of pre-acceptance checks is presented as a key publisher responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility to update the publication record
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher takes responsibility for updating the publication record when concerns are identified after publication (including retractions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer Nature cites updating the publication record when concerns are found; the article quantifies that 2,923 articles were retracted in the prior year as part of that corrective activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about integrity processes and statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should be transparent about how accuracy and integrity are maintained and share data (e.g., number of retractions) to demonstrate commitment to scientific integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer Nature published a research integrity page with data (retraction counts, breakdown by publication date and OA status) to increase transparency; commenters dispute whether such summary data is sufficient without detailed process transparency and staffing information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicious citations as an indicator of concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspicious citation patterns can trigger integrity investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites 'suspicious citations' as one reason Environmental Science and Pollution Research cleaned up hundreds of papers. Suspicious citation behavior is presented as a concrete red flag that may warrant further scrutiny or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tortured phrases / nonsensical language as a red flag
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of 'tortured phrases' or unusual, nonsensical wording in manuscripts is an indicator of problematic papers (e.g., possible paper mills or AI misuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references 'an article full of tortured phrases' and other instances where tortured phrases prompted concern; this is presented as an observable quality issue that can trigger investigation or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undisclosed use of AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Undisclosed use of AI in articles is a trigger for integrity concerns and possible corrective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Environmental Science and Pollution Research flagged 'undisclosed use of AI' among the issues prompting clean-up; undisclosed AI usage is treated as an integrity breach when not declared per journal/publisher policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid authorship / improper authorship practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns over paid authorship (guest or ghost authorship, authorship-for-sale) are a ground for investigation and potential retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific Reports had retractions related to 'concerns over paid authorship'; paid authorship is cited as a concrete integrity violation detected post-publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems in special guest-edited issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Special issues or guest-edited issues can be vulnerable to systemic problems and may require additional scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied Nanoscience retracted 34 papers from special guest-edited issues described as 'riddled with problems,' indicating that special issues are a contextual risk factor for integrity breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest (editorial COI) as an integrity problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Undisclosed conflicts of interest, including editors appearing as co-authors across multiple chapters or articles, are flagged as problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter noted an editor being co-author on many chapters and questioned how hard it is to check for editor-in-chief names among article titles, pointing to editorial COI as a quality/control failure mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate monitoring capacity and staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective monitoring of journal integrity requires sufficient trained staff and resources; lack of staffing undermines oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters questioned how a publisher can monitor 3,000 journals and observed that monitoring would require paying people; one commenter noted Springer Nature previously indicated 30 research integrity staff, implying that staffing levels are material to the effectiveness of integrity oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of downstream citations to retracted papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that cite retracted articles should be reviewed and, where appropriate, retracted or issued an expression of concern to avoid propagation of tainted findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters asked why papers citing retracted work aren't also retracted or at least issued expressions of concern, likening the problem to a 'poisonous tree' doctrine—suggesting a criterion that downstream literature be assessed and corrected where affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and reviewer accountability / sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reviewers who fail in their duties (e.g., allow dubious papers through) should face accountability measures, such as debarment or suspension from editorial/peer-review activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters proposed debarment or banning of editors/reviewers who allowed problematic papers, recommending corrective sanctions as a deterrent and accountability mechanism; this is presented as a community expectation rather than a publisher policy on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quality-control tools and defined investigation processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should deploy tools and follow defined processes for quality control, for identifying what prompts an investigation and for conducting investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states Springer Nature's page 'outlines the tools the publisher uses for quality control, what prompts a research integrity investigation, and what happens during such investigations.' The specific tools/processes are not detailed in the article but are described as an explicit part of publisher practice.
